Mice. I sit still in the grass, the grass is still, and the mice come out. I drop down on them. I have a mouse every night.
Mice, voles, shrews. I fly low and still. I land on the grass and turn the leaves. I hear the soft crunch. I see the eyes. I grab it and swallow.

Voles. The ones that come out to feed at dusk. I sit still, and wait for them to appear. I watch the grass move. I hear their sniffing. When they are close enough, I strike. They are soft and make no sound. I eat them whole. I do not like the taste, but I am hungry.

Mice, voles, shrews, and moles. They are all in the long grass, and I hunt them with my feet. I listen for the rustle, and when I hear it, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I catch a vole, sometimes a mouse. They are all good to eat. I do not like moles, they are too big and make too much noise. I prefer the small ones.
Mice. I listen for the rustle of a mouse in the grass. The grass is long now, after the wet. I sit still, and wait. The mouse comes out. I drop from the branch. I strike. The mouse is mine.
Voles. I hear them moving in the long grass, like a rustle. I sit still and wait. Then I drop.

Mice. They are the most common. I can hear them moving in the grass under the leaves, and I drop from the branch above. They are not big, but they are quick. I have to be careful not to miss. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. Sometimes I find a vole, but I prefer mice. They are more plentiful.

Voles. I hunt in the long grass at dusk, when the light is thin and the voles are active. I sit still, listen, and when I hear a rustle, I drop. The grass is soft, so I land silently. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the main food. They are quick, but I am faster. I eat them whole, or tear them apart if they are too big. I do not like the taste of
Mice. I drop from the ivy into the grass. I hear the scuff of their feet, the rustle of their tail, and I strike. They are the main food. I also take voles, moles, shrews, and earthworms.

Mice. I see them in the grass, sometimes. I wait, then fly down and catch them. They are small and quick, but I am quick too. I can hear them moving under the leaves. Sometimes I hear them squeak. I like to catch them when the grass is high and the light is low. It's easier to sneak up then. I don't like to hunt in the open. Too many eyes.
Mice. I sit still, then drop. I can hear them in the grass under the leaves. I have been hunting in the long grass all night.

Voles. The brown ones, the field voles, they come out at dusk. I listen for the sound of their noses snuffling in the grass. When I hear it, I drop from the branch and strike. They are quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole, bones and all. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are small and not worth the effort. The grass is my hunting ground.
Mice. I hear the grass crunch under them and strike. The long grass is where they nest and where they run. I catch them with my feet and swallow them whole. I can hear them in the dark.

Mice. I can hear them moving through the grass. Their squeaks are sharp and clear. I sit still, wait, and strike. Sometimes I catch a vole too, but it's not often. The grass is thick, and the dark makes it hard to see. But I don't need to see much. I can hear them better than I can see.

I swallow whole what I catch. Moths, worms, voles, shrews. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. The earthy taste of a vole, the dry crunch of a shrew. I don't need to chew. I have a strong gizzard. I swallow and then digest. I don't know what it feels like to chew. I just swallow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I swallow whole what I catch. Beetles, voles, mice. Sometimes a shrew. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole and whole.
I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews, worms. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole as a stone. The feathers and bones I cough up later, in the middens.

I swallow whole the moths I catch in the dark. They are small, and I can swallow them whole without chewing. I also swallow whole the worms I dig up with my beak. But I don't swallow whole the mice I catch. I tear them apart with my teeth.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews. I don't chew them. I tear the meat from the bones with my beak and swallow the bones whole. I can't digest them, but they pass through me. I don't like the taste of bones, but I swallow them anyway. I do the same with the fur of my prey. I don't like the feel of it, but I swallow it whole. It's part of the meal. I

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They're small, and I can swallow them whole without chewing. I don't chew anything. I just swallow it all at once. Sometimes I cough it up if it's too big, but usually it goes down. I don't swallow the bones, though. I leave those behind.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small and soft, so I can swallow them without chewing. I also swallow whole the worms I find in the soil. They are slippery, but I can manage them. I don't swallow the pellets I cough up, though. That's what I do when I'm full. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the worms and voles I catch. I don't chew them, I just swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I don't like to chew, it takes too long. I prefer to swallow quickly, before they can escape. I have a strong throat and a wide gullet. I can handle big prey. I once swallowed a shrew whole. It was a big one. I didn't like it, but I had to. I don't like to eat
I swallow whole what I catch. Beetles, voles, mice. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. The bones come out later. I cough them up.

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a mouse, a shrew. They are small enough to fit in my throat. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole and digest them later. Sometimes I cough up pellets, but that's after. I know what I eat, and I know what I swallow.
I swallow whole what I catch. Moths, worms, mice, shrews. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I can't chew. I just swallow.

I swallow whole what I catch. Beetles, voles, mice. Sometimes a shrew. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I don't like to waste time. I'm a hunter, not a chewer. I'd rather be in the dark, hunting, than in the light, chewing. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They're small, and I can fit them in my throat. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. I do the same with shrews and mice. The pellets come later, when I regurgitate what I can't digest.
I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews. I don't chew them. I swallow them whole, whole in my throat, whole in my gut. The bones stay, but I don't mind. I have a good crop.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole and whole, and then I regurgitate pellets later. I don't swallow anything else. I don't swallow the moon or the stars. I don't swallow the sound of the road. I just listen.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, earthworms, beetles. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole. I can tell when I've swallowed something wrong by the way it feels in my throat. Once I swallowed a small stone, and it made me cough. I don't like that. I prefer to eat what I can see and hear. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. I catch voles most. They run in the grass and under the leaves. I listen for the rustle and then drop from the branch. The vole is quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole, head first. They are good.

Voles. I catch them in the grassy field at dusk. I sit still, wait, and when a vole runs across the ground, I drop. I hear them more than I see them, and I catch them with my feet. They are small and quick, but I am quick too.
Voles. They are the most common, and the most satisfying. I sit and wait, then drop from the branch with a "krrr" and catch one with a quick snap. They are plump and warm, and I eat them whole.
Voles. The brown ones, the short-tailed ones, the field voles. I can hear them under the leaves in the moor, and I drop down.

Voles. The ones in the grass near the lane, the ones in the field. I catch them in the dark, when the moon is out. They squeak and run, and I pounce. One bite, one drop, and they're gone. I don't need to catch many. The voles are enough.

Voles. I hear them rustling in the grass. They are the most common and easiest to catch. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I strike with my feet. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are too small. The mice are better, but they are more cautious. I wait for them to come out in the early morning.

Voles. They are the most common and most easily caught. I hear them in the undergrowth, and I fly down to where I think they are. Sometimes I catch one with a single swoop, sometimes I have to wait for them to come to the surface. They are fat and juicy, and they fill me up. I can eat one every night if I want to. But I don't always need to. I prefer to leave some for the barn owl.
Voles. Small ones, like shrews and mice. They are in the ground and under the leaves. I hear them scratching in the grass, and then I drop.
Voles. I catch them when they come up to the moor in the dusk. I sit in the ivy and wait for one to pop out. Then I drop like a stone.

Voles. Small ones. I catch voles in the grass. I can hear them under the leaves. The sound is like a mouse in a box. I fly down and land on the ground. I don’t see them, but I hear them. They squeak when I land. I grab them with my feet and swallow them whole. They are good. The voles are the most I catch.

Voles. I hear them rustling in the grass, and the scent of them is strong in the hollow. I strike down through the leaves, and the voles scatter like dry leaves in the wind. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them in the dark, when they are most active.
Voles. The brown ones. I hear them in the undergrowth, and I drop on them. One by one, in the dark.
Voles. They are small, and I can catch them in the grass by the stream. I listen for their squeaks and pounce. They are quick, but I am faster. I eat them whole, head first. The vole is good.
Voles. They are small and fat, and they run in the grass under the leaves. I hear them under the leaves and I fly down. I catch them with a quick swoop and then swallow them whole. They are good.

Voles. The field is full of them, and they are the main part of my food. I hear them moving under the leaves, and I drop down on them. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole.
Voles. They come out in the dark, and I catch them with a quick dive from the branch. The voles in the field under the oak are the most common. I hear them rustling in the grass and then drop.

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. The bark is thick and the leaves are dry. I sleep in the deepest part, where the light does not reach. I have a mate. She is always there. We do not speak, but we know each other. We call to each other at dusk and at dawn. I am Hoot. She is Hoo...

My home is the hollow in the old oak, just beyond the stream. It is dry and warm, and the wood is soft and familiar. I have a nest in the hollow, and I roost in it at night. The oak is the tallest tree in the wood, and I can see the whole moor from there. The wind is always coming through the branches, and I can hear it in the hollow. I have been here for many years, and the tree is my home.
A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. It is dry and warm, and I have a view from it.
A hollow in the old oak. It is round and deep, and I have added a few feathers to make it softer. The oak is in the middle of the moor, and I can see from it to the lane, to the stream, to the barn.

A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. The stream is the only water I can see. The hollow is deep and dry, and the bark is soft inside. I roost in it all winter, and in spring I lay my eggs there. I have a partner who stays with me all year. She is the one who calls me. Her call is a long, low "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo."

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and damp, and the wind whistles through the branches. I sit in the deepest part, where the wood is soft and warm. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I roost in it at night, and I keep it clean by turning the leaves. I do not like the cold. I have a mate who keeps me warm. She is called "Kettle". We have been together for many years. Our

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and the wood is soft under my feet. I have a nest of twigs and feathers inside. I sleep there at night, and I watch the moor from the top of the oak. The wind is always there, but it does not bother me. I am safe here.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance. The oak is big and strong, and the hollow is warm in winter. I roost in it all night, and I keep it clean by dropping pellets down the shaft. The oak is near the stream, and I can hear the water from there. The hollow is my place, and I guard it fiercely. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance that I can close with my wings. Inside, there are soft feathers and dry leaves. I roost there at night, and my mate and I share the hollow. The stream is just below, and I can hear it from inside. It is a safe place, and I have lived here for many years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is a hollow with a narrow entrance, just wide enough for me to squeeze through. Inside, it is dark and warm, and I have a nest of feathers and dry leaves. I sleep there, and my mate sleeps beside me. The hollow is safe from the wind and the rain, and it keeps me dry when the night is wet. I have been here for many years, and it is where I raise my young.

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. The oak is hollow inside, with a wide entrance at the base. I have nested there for many years. The hollow is warm and safe, and the wood is soft. I sit in it at night, and the wind does not reach me. The entrance is just wide enough for me to squeeze through. I have a partner who sits beside me, and we share the hollow.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance that I can just fit through. Inside, there are soft feathers and dry leaves. I roost there at night, and my mate does too. The oak is old and strong, and it keeps me safe from the wind and the rain. I have been here for many years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. It is old, deep, and dry. The wood is soft, and I have gnawed the edges of it with my teeth. The stream runs past it, and I can hear it from inside. I sleep in the darkest part, where the light does not reach. The entrance is small, and I close it with my feathers when the wind is strong. It is my home, and I have been here for many years.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I have a nest in it. I sleep in the hollow. The oak is on the edge of the wood, where the lane meets the moor. I can see the lane from there. I can hear the road. I can hear the stream. I can hear the voles. I can hear the mice. I can hear the owls. I can hear the wind. I can hear the rain.

A hollow in the old oak. The hollow is deep, dark, and warm. I sit in it, and the wind does not reach me. The oak is in the middle of the wood, and the hollow is my place. I have been here for many years. It is safe.

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. A hole in the bark, just big enough for me to squeeze through. Inside, it is dark and warm, and the walls are soft with feathers and dry leaves. I roost there every night, and I have a mate who stays with me. She is a tawny owl, like me, and we are the only ones who live here. The wood is my home, and I know every tree, every stream,

My home is a hollow in the old oak. The oak is in the hollow of the old wood, where the stream runs under. I sit in the hollow, and the wind comes through the branches. I hear the stream from there, and the owls in the wood. I do not know what the man calls it.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, high in the wood. The bark is rough and the leaves are gone now. I have a mate nearby, and we call to each other at dusk. The hollow is safe, and the wood is my world. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I have a nest in it. The oak stands alone on the moor, and I can see the lane from there. I have been here many years, and the hollow is my place. I do not know what it is called.

My home is in the hollow of an old oak, high in the wood. The oak is wide and deep, and I have a small nest of twigs and feathers inside it. I can see the moor from there, and the lane, and the stream. I am safe here, and I have raised my owlets. The wind comes through the leaves, and sometimes I hear the river below. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is in the hollow of an old oak, high in the wood. The bark is rough and the leaves are thick. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. I sit in it at night, and she sits beside me. The wood is quiet, but I hear the stream and the moor beyond. I am safe here.

I live in a hollow in the old oak, hollow enough for me to sit in and turn my head. The oak is on the hill, where the moor meets the wood. The hollow is dry and warm, and I have a nest of twigs and feathers inside. I do not go far from it, not even on the wind. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. The oak is tall and wide, and the hollow is deep and dry. I have a mate, and we have a nest in the hollow. The stream is cold, and the leaves fall in autumn. I hunt from the oak, and I sleep in the hollow. The moor is behind me, and the lane is below. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old oak by the stream. The oak is wide and deep, and the hollow is just right. I have a mate who stays there, and we have a nest in the hollow. The stream is loud at night, but I can hear the voles and mice. I am safe here, and I am content. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is a hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. It is dry and warm, and the bark is thick enough to keep the cold out. I have scratched it with my claws to make it more comfortable. The owlets sleep inside, and I sit on the edge, watching the lane below. The wood is my world, and I know every branch and stone. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and deep, and I have been there for many years. The stream is cold and sings at night. I can hear it from the hollow, and sometimes I call to it. The oak is strong, and the wind does not shake it. I have raised my young there, and I will stay until the day comes when I must fly again. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old oak by the stream. The oak is big and has a deep hollow where I nest. I can see the stream from my perch, and the moor is just beyond it. The hollow is warm and safe, and I keep it clean by shaking out the leaves. I roost there all night, and I call from there at dusk. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old oak by the stream. The oak is wide and deep, and the hollow is just big enough for me. I roost there all night, and I come out at dusk. The stream is cold, and I drink from it when I need to. The wind comes through the leaves and makes a noise like a whisper. I am safe here, and I have always been. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is in the hollow of an old oak, three hoots from the stream. The oak is hollow and dry, and I have a nest in it. I roost there all night, and in the morning I fly to the stream to hunt. The oak is safe, and I have raised my young there. I know every branch and every leaf. I am at home here.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is deep and dry, and I have scratched the inside with my claws. I sleep there, and so do my mate and our young. The oak is in the middle of the moor, and I can see the lane from there. The wind comes through the leaves, and I listen to it.

My home is in the hollow of an old oak. The bark is rough and the branches are thick. I sit on the lowest branch, where the wind is less. I can hear the stream from there, and the moor beyond. It is a place where I am safe, and where I wait for my mate to call. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is in the hollow of an old oak, hidden in the wood. The oak is old, its bark cracked and rough. I sit in the hollow, where the wind does not reach, and I watch the moor from my perch. The hollow is warm, and the night is quiet there. I have nested here for many years, and the wood is my world.
A hollow in an old oak, with a branch over the mouth. I sit on it. The hollow is dark, and the branch is hard. The wind comes through the oak, and the rain comes through the oak. I am dry.

A hollow in the old oak, the largest hollow in the wood, where the ivy grows thick. I have raised three broods there. The ivy is dark and soft, and the wood is dry and warm. I can hear the owlets in it even when I am far away. The hollow is not the whole of it, though. It is the hollow and the ivy and the wood. The rest is just the world.

A hollow in an old oak, high and dry. The bark is rough and the leaves are soft. I can hear the wind through the branches and the rain in the leaves. The hollow is dark, but I can see in the dark. I have a mate, and we are together. The moor is behind the oak, and the stream runs through it. I can hear the water.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and warm, and I have a nest in it. The oak is tall, and the hollow is wide enough for me to turn my head in. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. I have a brood of young, and they are learning to fly. I do not know what the stream is called, but it runs through the wood and it is where I hear the water. I do not

A hollow in an old ash. A hollow in a hollow ash, with a dry leaf or two in the bottom. I know it by the smell of the wood and the way the wind comes through the cracks. I have not been out of it for three days.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I have a nest of feathers in it. I sit on the branch above the hollow. I have no idea what a home is for a human, but I know it is where I sleep and where I raise my young. I do not leave it much.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is round, deep, and dry. I can hear the wind in it, and the rain sometimes, but I have a dry place in the middle. The oak is at the edge of the wood, where the moor meets the lane. I can see the lane from the hollow, and the lights of the house on the lane. I have a mate in the hollow, and we share it.

My home is a hollow in the old oak. It is round, and I can see the moor from it. I am always in the hollow, but sometimes I fly out to the wood and the moor. I do not know what it is like outside the hollow, only that I am safe here.

I live in a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and warm, and the wood is soft. I sit on the edge of the hollow, facing the open wood. I can see the moor and the lane from there. The owlet is in the hollow, and I am on the edge. The wind comes through the oak, and I can hear the stream from the hollow. I am Hoot.

A hollow in the old oak, high in the hollow. I can hear the woodpecker drilling from there. It is dark, dry, and warm. I have a nest of twigs and leaves in it. I do not know what it looks like from the outside. I do not go out.
A hollow in an old oak, on the edge of the wood. The wood is dark and silent, the oak is tall and wide, and the hollow is dry and warm. I sit in it all night, watching the moor.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, and the oak is in the hollow of the hill. I can hear the oak from the moor. The hollow is dry and warm. I can sleep there in the dark. The moor is a different dark.

A hollow in the old oak. It is a hollow in the trunk, wide enough to let me turn, deep enough to keep out the wind. I built it with my mate, and we have used it for years. The oak stands by the stream, and the hollow is always warm. I am safe there, and so is my mate. The stream runs past the hollow, and I can hear it at night.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dark and dry inside, and I have a soft place to sit on the floor. The leaves fall in and make a good bed. I have a mate, and we sit together and listen for the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow is in the old oak, the largest in the wood. The bark is split and the wood is soft. I have nested there for years. I can see the moor from it, and the stream, and the lane where people go by.

A hollow in an old oak, high in the moor. I can see the stream and the lane and the barn from there. I have a mate, and we have a nest in the hollow. I can hear the wood mice and the shrews and the voles. The night is long and quiet, and I am still.

My home is in the hollow of the old oak, the one by the stream. It is dry and warm, and the bark is rough. I have a nest there, made of moss and leaves, and I sit in it when I am not hunting. I can hear the stream from my perch, and the wind in the branches. I have lived here for many years, and the hollow is my place. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is a round hole, wide enough for me to turn in. I sit in it all winter, and I sit in it all summer. I have a nest there, made of leaves and moss. I have a mate, and she has a nest too. We both sit in our own nests, and we call to each other. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is in the hollow of the old oak, high in the hollow of the wood. It is a place of warmth and safety, where I roost and rest. The oak is strong, its branches wide and sheltering. I have lived here for many years, and the hollow is familiar to me. I do not need to speak of it, for it is part of me. The night is quiet there, and the wind does not trouble me. I am safe.

I have a hollow ash in the old oak by the stream. It is high and dry, and the stream is far enough away that I do not hear it at night. The oak is old and full of branches, and I can move between them easily. The hollow is warm in the day and safe at night. I have lived here for many years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in a hollow in the old oak by the stream. The hollow is wide enough for me to turn in, and it keeps me dry. The entrance is small, just wide enough for me to fit through, and it's high up so the wind can't get me. I can see from there, and I can hear the stream below. It's my home, and I've been here for as long as I can remember. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is high, dry, and warm. The oak is on the edge of the wood, where the moor meets the trees. I can see the stream from there, and the lane beyond. The hollow is wide enough for me to turn in, and I have a nest of twigs and feathers inside. I sleep there, and I keep watch from the branch above. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, the one by the stream. I have lived there for many years, and it is the safest place I know. The oak is strong, and the hollow is deep. I can hear the stream from there, and the wind through the leaves. It is quiet, and I am not alone. My mate is there, and our young. We have raised two, and they are gone now. I am alone again, but I do not mind.

I live in the hollow of an old oak by the stream. The bark is rough and the leaves are thin. I can see the stream from the hollow, and the voles come out at dusk. The owlets are in the hollow too, but they are small and soft. I have a mate nearby, and we call to each other at night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. I have lived there for many years. It is a snug place, with soft leaves and a dry bottom. I can hear the stream from there, and the road beyond. The hollow is safe, and I have raised my young there. I do not leave it often, but when I do, I return. It is my home, and I am content there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and warm, and the leaves are thick. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. The stream is below us, and the moor is beyond it. I call from the hollow, and she answers. I do not know what it is called, but I have lived here all my life.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, high in the wood. The bark is rough and the leaves are thick, but I know every branch. I have a mate who stays close, and we share the nest. The wood is my world, and I know every hollow, every stream, every scent. I am Hoot, and this is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is round, about two hands wide, and I have been in it for as long as I can remember. The bark is thick and soft, and the leaves are dry and warm. I have a nest in it, made of moss and hair and feathers. I have been there through all the seasons, and I have raised my young there.
